blocks.text: The thirteenth day of Adar arrived—the very day enemies of the Jews hoped to destroy them. But the situation reversed completely: instead of falling to their enemies, the Jews found themselves in position to defend against those who hated them. Throughout King Ahasuerus's provinces, Jews gathered in their cities to confront those seeking their harm. The reversal was decisive and total.

The Jews struck down their enemies with the sword throughout the provinces. In the fortress of Shushan, they killed five hundred. Ten sons of Haman—Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha—were slain. Remarkably, despite their decisive military victory and clear authority to plunder the defeated, the Jews did not take spoils from those they defeated. This disciplined restraint in victory demonstrates that their resistance was self-defense, not conquest.

When King Ahasuerus learned of the deaths in Shushan and the slaying of Haman's ten sons, he granted Esther an extraordinary petition: the Jews in Shushan would be permitted to continue their self-defense for one additional day, and Haman's ten sons would be hanged publicly. This extension ensured complete neutralization of the threat that had been arranged against the Jewish people.
